stem: Which three components are the minimum needed to discover a service of baseline-supported operating systems, infrastructure, and applications?

options.text: MID Server, IP Range, and Subnet Mask
MID Server, IP Range, and Entry Point
MID Server, Entry Point, and Credentials
MID Server, Entry Point, and Subnet Mask

rationale: Top-down discovery needs a worker, a starting point, and a way in: the MID Server runs the probes, the Entry Point tells it where the service begins, and Credentials let it authenticate to each host it reaches. Without any one of the three, discovery can't complete.

distractor_notes.A: IP range and subnet mask scope a network sweep but supply no entry point and, crucially, no credentials.
distractor_notes.B: An IP range is optional for top-down mapping; the missing essential here is credentials.
distractor_notes.D: A subnet mask only scopes traffic; without credentials the MID Server can't gather service details.

stem: What information is required to discover a service in Service Mapping?

options.text: Credentials, MID Server, and Entry Point
MID Server, IP Range, and Load Balancer
MID Server, Network Diagram, and Entry Point
Credentials, Application name, and MID Server

rationale: Same essential trio: credentials to authenticate, a MID Server to execute, and an entry point to know where to start. Everything else (diagrams, app names) is helpful context but not what the engine strictly needs to begin.

distractor_notes.B: An IP range/load balancer can serve as an entry point but this option omits credentials.
distractor_notes.C: A network diagram is a human artifact, not an input the engine consumes.
distractor_notes.D: An application name isn't required to start; the engine needs an entry point to begin.

stem: Which are valid methods to initiate discovery of a service?

options.text: Map multiple services by importing entry points from a CSV file
Map services suggested by discovering MID Servers
Map multiple services suggested by discovering enterprise load balancers
Map a single service by configuring one entry point
Map services from assets stored in the CMDB

rationale: You start mapping by giving Service Mapping entry points: one at a time (single entry point), in bulk (CSV import), or by letting it suggest candidates from discovered load balancers (their VIPs are natural service front doors). All three are documented ways to kick off discovery.

distractor_notes.B: MID Servers are infrastructure that runs discovery; discovering them doesn't suggest services to map.
distractor_notes.E: Assets aren't the basis for suggesting service maps; entry points are.

stem: Which address is required for Service Mapping to discover a load balancer that doesn't yet exist in the CMDB?
rationale: To discover a network device like a load balancer, Service Mapping must reach its management interface — the management IP. That's the address the MID Server uses to log in, run commands, and read the device's configuration and pools.

distractor_notes.B: There is no 'MIB address'; a MIB is an SNMP data structure, not an address.
distractor_notes.C: A MAC address is layer-2 and isn't routable for management access.
distractor_notes.D: A public IP isn't required and often isn't how internal devices are managed.

stem: Which format is valid when entering SSH private key credentials in ServiceNow?
rationale: ServiceNow stores SSH private keys in PEM format (the standard ----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY---- block). You paste the PEM key into the credential record and the MID Server uses it to authenticate to Unix/Linux targets over SSH.

distractor_notes.A: PMI is a project-management institute/term, not a key format.
distractor_notes.B: PDP is not a key format (it's a policy decision point in access control).
distractor_notes.C: PGP is for message encryption/signing, not SSH private key storage here.

stem: When configuring SNMP credentials for discovery, which two statements are true?

options.text: SNMP v1, v2c, and v3 are supported
A read/write SNMP account is required
A read-only SNMP account is sufficient for discovery

rationale: Discovery only reads device data over SNMP, so a read-only community/account is enough, and the platform supports v1, v2c, and v3 so you can match the device's security posture. Read/write would grant more than discovery needs.

distractor_notes.B: Read/write is unnecessary; discovery never changes device configuration.
distractor_notes.C: v3 is supported too, adding authentication and encryption.

stem: An application (Ignite) requires credentials different from the host OS. How should you enter them?

options.text: Use the Change user operation to hardcode them in the pattern
Add a credential of type 'Other' with no CI type
Store the credentials as attributes on the Ignite CI
Add a credential of type 'Applicative' and associate the appropriate CI type for Ignite

rationale: Application-level logins use the Applicative credential type, tied to the relevant CI type so the engine knows when to use them. That keeps app credentials separate from the host OS credentials and applies them only where appropriate.

distractor_notes.A: Change user handles privilege elevation mid-pattern, not initial application credential storage.
distractor_notes.B: 'Other' is a generic catch-all and, without a CI-type association, won't be applied to Ignite as intended.
distractor_notes.C: Credentials are never stored as CI attributes — that's both insecure and unsupported.

stem: To discover UNIX targets with least privilege, which SSH credential approach is recommended?

options.text: A non-root account granted selective sudo
Domain access with local administrator rights

rationale: Best practice is a non-root user that can run only the specific commands discovery needs via sudo. It satisfies discovery while honoring least-privilege security policies that typically forbid handing out root.

distractor_notes.A: WMI is the Windows management interface, not an SSH/UNIX credential.
distractor_notes.C: Domain/local-admin are Windows concepts, irrelevant to SSH on UNIX.
distractor_notes.D: Root is more access than discovery needs and is usually disallowed by security.

stem: What is created after a credential is successfully used for the first time to access a device?

options.text: A credential affinity linking that device to the working credential

rationale: Credential affinity remembers which credential worked for a given target, so future runs go straight to it instead of cycling through every credential again. That speeds up discovery and reduces failed-login noise.

distractor_notes.B: The credential store is a pre-existing structure, not generated on first success.
distractor_notes.C: There's no 'credential lock' artifact created at first use.
distractor_notes.D: The vault is where credentials are stored; it isn't created per first-successful-use.

stem: Checks are scanned at branches, sent via web service through an F5, processed by Apache then an ImageSmart app server, and stored in Oracle. Tellers also log in to ImageSmart through a Citrix portal to review checks. How many business services and entry points is this?

options.text: Two services and two entry points
Two services and one entry point
One service and two entry points
One service and one entry point

rationale: The whole flow delivers one business outcome — process a deposited check — so it's one service. But it can be entered two ways: the external scan/web-service capture, and the teller's Citrix login to review. Each distinct way in is its own entry point, giving one service with two entry points.

distractor_notes.A: It's a single service; the two access paths are entry points, not separate services.
distractor_notes.B: The internal stages all serve one logical service; they aren't two services.
distractor_notes.D: There are two distinct ways to enter the service (capture vs. teller review), not one.

stem: Which list best represents a typical multi-tier service architecture?

options.text: Load Balancer > Web Server Cluster > Application Server Cluster > Database
Load Balancer > Web Server Cluster > Database > Application Server Cluster
Load Balancer > WebSphere MQ > Database > Web Server Cluster
Load Balancer > Web Server Cluster > Middleware > Database > Application Server Cluster

rationale: Traffic flows presentation → logic → data: the load balancer fronts the web tier, the web tier hands off to the application tier, and the application tier reads/writes the database last. The database sits at the back, isolated behind the app logic.

distractor_notes.B: This puts the database before the application tier, reversing the normal processing order.
distractor_notes.C: Inserting WebSphere MQ here and ending at the web tier scrambles the standard layering.
distractor_notes.D: Placing middleware before the app tier and DB before the app cluster misorders the tiers.

stem: Which module do you use to convert legacy business services into application services in bulk rather than one at a time?
rationale: The Application Services module includes the bulk-convert action that turns many legacy business services into application services at once. The other navigation areas list or define things but don't expose the bulk conversion workflow.

distractor_notes.A: Applications navigates definitions; it lacks the bulk-convert action.
distractor_notes.B: Business Applications is a catalog view without conversion tooling.
distractor_notes.C: A generic Services list doesn't offer bulk conversion.

stem: What value is set in the Discovery source field when an application is discovered by Service Mapping?
rationale: Service Mapping stamps its discovered CIs with the Discovery source 'Service Mapping', distinguishing them from records created by horizontal Discovery or other integrations. That source value matters for reconciliation rules and data lineage.

distractor_notes.B: 'ServiceNow' is generic/manual, not the Service Mapping source.
distractor_notes.C: 'Discovery' is the horizontal discovery source, a different engine.
distractor_notes.D: 'Application Service' is a CI category, not a discovery source value.

stem: A customer wants to track a new hardware CI in a dedicated new table where no baseline class fits. What should be done?

options.text: Create a new table that extends Task [task]
Create a new table that extends Configuration Item [cmdb_ci]
Create a new table that extends Application [cmdb_ci_appl]

rationale: New CI classes should extend cmdb_ci so they inherit the generic CI attributes, relationships, and out-of-the-box CMDB/Service Mapping behavior. Extending the base CI table is the supported way to model a CI type the baseline hierarchy doesn't cover.

distractor_notes.A: Task models work items, not CIs; it lacks CI attributes and relationships.
distractor_notes.C: cmdb_ci_appl is for application CIs; using it for hardware forces the wrong model.
distractor_notes.D: Custom CI classes are permitted and supported when no baseline class fits.

stem: Within the CMDB, application CI classes are children of which parent class?
rationale: cmdb_ci_appl is the base class for application CIs; specialized application types (web servers, app servers, databases as services) extend from it. That's why querying cmdb_ci_appl returns the whole family of discovered applications.

distractor_notes.A: Database Instance is itself a specialized application type, not the parent of all apps.
distractor_notes.B: cmdb_ci_software is a broader software class, not the direct parent of application CIs.
distractor_notes.D: Installed Software tracks installed packages, not running application CIs.

stem: Which of the following can serve as an entry point for a Service Mapping discovery?

options.text: A URL, host name, or IP address

rationale: Entry points describe where a service is reached — typically a URL, a hostname, or an IP/port. Service Mapping starts there and discovers downstream. The entry point type then dictates which patterns are eligible to run.

distractor_notes.A: A health KPI is a data-quality metric, not a place a service is accessed.
distractor_notes.C: A MID Server executes discovery; it isn't the service's access surface.
distractor_notes.D: An incident number is a record reference, not an entry point.

stem: What is the primary purpose of a schedule on an application service in Service Mapping?

options.text: To set the CMDB Health pass threshold
To choose the entry point type
To define which credentials are valid
To periodically rediscover the service so the map stays current as the environment changes

rationale: Schedules keep maps honest over time by re-running discovery on a cadence. Environments drift — new nodes, version changes, retired hosts — and a scheduled rediscovery captures those changes so the service map reflects reality rather than a one-time snapshot.

distractor_notes.A: Health thresholds are configured in CMDB Health, unrelated to a service schedule.
distractor_notes.B: Entry point type is set on the entry point, not by the schedule.
distractor_notes.C: Credential validity is managed in the credential store, not by a schedule.

stem: What is a Service Group used for in Service Mapping?

options.text: To organize related application services together for management and reporting

rationale: Service Groups bundle related application services so teams can manage, secure, and report on them as a set — for example all services owned by one business unit. It's an organizational grouping layered over individual service maps.

distractor_notes.B: Keys live in credential records, not service groups.
distractor_notes.C: Reconciliation precedence is a CMDB/IRE setting, unrelated to service groups.
distractor_notes.D: MID Server upgrades are managed separately, not via service groups.

stem: During pattern execution you must elevate to a different account to run a privileged command. Which operation handles this?

options.text: Change user (switch to elevated credentials mid-pattern)

rationale: The Change user operation switches the execution context to a different credential during a pattern, so a step that needs elevated rights can run while the rest of the pattern uses the standard account. It's about privilege elevation within a run, not storing the initial credential.

distractor_notes.A: Set Variable assigns a value; it doesn't change the execution account.
distractor_notes.C: Create Connection builds a relationship, unrelated to credential context.
distractor_notes.D: Parse File extracts text; it doesn't elevate privileges.

stem: A target host already exists in the CMDB when Service Mapping runs. What happens to that host?

options.text: It is skipped and never touched
It is duplicated to preserve history
It is rediscovered and only its changed attributes are updated
It is deleted and recreated as a new record

rationale: Service Mapping triggers host discovery as part of mapping, but IRE matches the existing CI and updates only what changed, preserving the same sys_id and its relationships. No churn, no duplicates — just an in-place refresh.

distractor_notes.A: The host is rediscovered, not skipped — that's how attributes stay current.
distractor_notes.B: Duplicating is exactly what IRE prevents through identification.
distractor_notes.D: Delete-and-recreate would break relationships and history; IRE updates in place.

stem: An entry point's first target is an application load balancer, but the load balancer isn't discovered. What is the key cause?

options.text: The entry point uses a user-facing IP instead of a management IP
No valid credential is configured for the load balancer
No Connection Section exists to downstream CIs

rationale: If the device itself doesn't get discovered at all, the engine couldn't authenticate to it — a missing or invalid credential. Connection logic and downstream identification only matter after the LB is reachable, so credentials are the first thing to check.

distractor_notes.A: The IP type affects what's reachable, but the documented key cause of non-discovery here is the credential.
distractor_notes.C: A missing connection section would hide downstream links, but the LB itself would still be discovered.
distractor_notes.D: Without identification the LB could still be reached and partially seen; total non-discovery points to access.

stem: Where are discovery credentials stored and managed in ServiceNow?

options.text: In the ECC Queue output records
As plain-text attributes on the target CI

rationale: Credentials live in the encrypted Credentials table managed by Credential Management; at run time the MID Server retrieves them to authenticate to targets. Centralizing and encrypting them is what keeps secrets out of patterns and CI records.

distractor_notes.A: Hardcoding secrets in patterns is insecure and unsupported.
distractor_notes.B: The ECC Queue carries probe payloads, not stored credentials.
distractor_notes.C: Credentials are never stored as CI attributes.

stem: Discovered application services in Service Mapping are stored in which table?
rationale: Service Mapping records each discovered service as an Application Service in cmdb_ci_service_discovered. That CI anchors the map's entry points and the relationships to all the underlying CIs that compose the service.

distractor_notes.A: cmdb_ci_server holds servers, not the service-level CI.
distractor_notes.B: cmdb_ci is the abstract base; discovered services land in the specific discovered-service table.
distractor_notes.C: task models work items, not services.

stem: A defined link between two CIs such as 'Runs on', 'Depends on', or 'Contains' is called what?
rationale: Runs on, Depends on, and Contains are all predefined Relationship Types in the CMDB. Service Mapping builds the service map by connecting CIs with these relationship types, which is what powers dependency and impact analysis.

distractor_notes.A: An attribute is a field value on a CI, not a link between two CIs.
distractor_notes.B: These relationship types apply broadly, not only application-to-application.
distractor_notes.D: 'CI Dependency value' isn't the term for these defined relationships.

stem: You need to start discovery for dozens of services at once. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Create each entry point manually one at a time
Import the entry points from a CSV file
Run a network-wide horizontal Discovery instead

rationale: CSV import is the supported bulk path: you list many entry points (IPs/URLs/hosts) in a file and Service Mapping creates and discovers them together. It's far faster than manual entry and is purpose-built for onboarding many services.

distractor_notes.A: Manual creation doesn't scale to dozens of services.
distractor_notes.B: Health thresholds have nothing to do with onboarding entry points.
distractor_notes.D: Horizontal Discovery inventories infrastructure; it doesn't map these services top-down from entry points.

stem: Which statement best describes a technical service modeled in Service Mapping?

options.text: An IT-facing service (e.g., DNS, authentication) that supports other services rather than being consumed directly by the business

rationale: Technical services are the shared, IT-facing capabilities (DNS, LDAP/auth, email relay) that other services depend on. Modeling them lets you reuse a shared dependency across many business services and analyze the blast radius if it fails.

distractor_notes.A: A workstation is an endpoint CI, not a shared technical service.
distractor_notes.B: A single table isn't a service; a database instance might be a CI it depends on.
distractor_notes.C: A landing page is content, not a modeled technical service.

stem: Before a pattern can classify a newly mapped application into the CMDB, what must exist as its destination?

options.text: A CI type/table for the application

rationale: Discovered data needs somewhere to land. The application's CI type/table defines that destination, so it must exist before the pattern can create or update the CI. Without a target class, the engine has nothing to populate.

distractor_notes.A: Incidents are operational records, unrelated to where a CI is stored.
distractor_notes.B: Health rules surface quality issues; they aren't a CI destination.
distractor_notes.D: A finished map is an output of discovery, not a precondition for classifying a CI.

stem: How does an application service differ from a legacy business service in Service Mapping?

options.text: An application service cannot be discovered
A business service can never relate to CIs
An application service is discovered/maintained with its dependency map and entry points

rationale: Application services are the modern, discoverable unit — they carry entry points and a maintained dependency map. Business services represent broader business offerings; ServiceNow encourages converting legacy business services into application services so they gain a real, maintained topology.

distractor_notes.A: Application services are precisely what Service Mapping discovers.
distractor_notes.B: They're related but distinct concepts, which is why a conversion path exists.
distractor_notes.C: Business services can relate to CIs; they're just modeled at a higher level.

stem: A device responds at a user-facing VIP but management actions fail. For Service Mapping to manage and fully discover it, which address should the entry point/credential target?

options.text: The broadcast address of the subnet

rationale: User-facing VIPs serve traffic but often don't expose management. To run commands and read configuration, Service Mapping needs the device's management interface — that's where administrative access lives. Pointing discovery at the management IP unblocks full discovery.

distractor_notes.A: The DNS server resolves names; it isn't the target device's management interface.
distractor_notes.C: The MID Server is the worker, not the device you're trying to manage.
distractor_notes.D: A broadcast address isn't a manageable device endpoint.

stem: What primarily distinguishes a Service Mapping service map from a simple inventory list of CIs?

options.text: It captures the relationships/dependencies among CIs, not just the CIs themselves
It stores CIs in a separate database from the CMDB

rationale: The value of a service map is the edges, not just the nodes. Service Mapping discovers how CIs depend on one another, turning a flat inventory into a dependency graph that supports impact analysis and root-cause work.

distractor_notes.A: It maps applications and services, not just hardware.
distractor_notes.C: Service maps live in the CMDB, not a separate database.
distractor_notes.D: Cloud resources are included, not excluded.

stem: You want a reusable, query-defined set of CIs (e.g., all CIs supporting one application) to target reporting and actions. Which construct fits?

options.text: A CMDB Group / Dynamic CI Group

rationale: A query-based CMDB/Dynamic CI Group defines a reusable population of CIs you can point reporting, certification, and lifecycle actions at — without rebuilding the same filter each time. It recomputes as the underlying data changes.

distractor_notes.B: A schedule controls when discovery runs, not a reusable CI population.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies affect form behavior, not CI scoping.
distractor_notes.D: Incident business rules act on incidents, not CMDB CI sets.

stem: How can you restrict a credential so it is only tried against certain devices or CI types?

options.text: Add it to the ECC Queue manually
Associate the credential with a specific CI type and/or MID Server / IP scope
Store it as plain text on each device

rationale: Credentials can be scoped — by CI type, by MID Server, or by IP/network range — so the engine only attempts them where they're relevant. Scoping reduces failed logins, account lockouts, and the time spent cycling through the wrong credentials.

distractor_notes.A: The ECC Queue carries payloads; you don't place credentials there.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling IRE corrupts identification and has nothing to do with credential scope.
distractor_notes.D: Plain-text on devices is insecure and not how ServiceNow stores credentials.

stem: What is the most direct way to map a single new service?

options.text: Configure one entry point for that service and run discovery
Run a full horizontal Discovery of the data center
Import a CSV of hundreds of entry points

rationale: For one service, you define its single entry point (URL/host/IP) and start discovery. Service Mapping follows the dependencies from that point and builds the map — no bulk import or full-environment sweep needed.

distractor_notes.B: Health rules measure data quality; they don't initiate a service map.
distractor_notes.C: Horizontal Discovery inventories infrastructure; it doesn't map one service top-down.
distractor_notes.D: CSV import is for bulk onboarding, overkill for a single service.

stem: By default, how often does the Heartbeat probe send a synthetic transaction to check a mapped service's entry point?
rationale: The Heartbeat runs a lightweight synthetic transaction against the entry point on a default 5-minute cadence — frequent enough to catch outages quickly without flooding the target. It's how Service Mapping keeps a near-real-time read on entry-point availability.

distractor_notes.A: 10 minutes is slower than the documented default.
distractor_notes.B: 30 minutes is the MID Server upgrade-check default, not the heartbeat interval.
distractor_notes.C: 1 minute would be unnecessarily aggressive and isn't the default.

stem: What is the purpose of the Service Mapping Heartbeat?

options.text: To verify that a mapped service's entry point is reachable/available over time

rationale: Heartbeat is an availability check: by periodically probing the entry point, it tells you whether the service's front door is still responding. That signal feeds operational awareness without a full rediscovery each time.

distractor_notes.B: Publishing patterns is unrelated to the heartbeat.
distractor_notes.C: MID Server upgrades are a separate process on their own schedule.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation is an IRE function, not the heartbeat's job.

stem: A noisy, irrelevant CI keeps appearing on a service map. How do you keep it off the map while leaving discovery otherwise intact?

options.text: Add it as an exclusion on the map
Delete the CI from the CMDB

rationale: Exclusions let you tell a specific map to ignore a CI or connection without deleting real data or breaking discovery elsewhere. The CI still exists in the CMDB; it just stops cluttering this service's view.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting the CI removes legitimate data and may break other maps that need it.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling IRE corrupts identification platform-wide.
distractor_notes.D: Removing the MID Server breaks all discovery, not just this CI.

stem: Which scheduled job is installed with the Service Mapping Plus (sn_sm_scoped_app) application?

options.text: Generate entry point candidates from NetFlow and netstat data
Update statistics for the application service readiness dashboard

rationale: Service Mapping Plus ships a scheduled job that refreshes the statistics behind the Application Service Readiness dashboard, keeping its readiness and confidence figures current. That dashboard is a core Plus feature, so its data-refresh job comes with it.

distractor_notes.A: Query-based service updates aren't this scoped app's dedicated scheduled job.
distractor_notes.B: NetFlow/netstat candidate generation belongs to traffic-based connections/ADM, not this job.
distractor_notes.C: Business service status updates aren't delivered as a Plus scheduled job.

stem: To discover most Windows hosts via WMI, what credential is typically sufficient?

options.text: An SSH key in PEM format
A domain user with local administrator rights on the target

rationale: Windows discovery uses WMI, which needs a domain account that holds local admin on the target so it can read system, service, and software information. SSH keys and SNMP communities apply to Unix/network devices, not WMI on Windows.

distractor_notes.A: SSH/PEM is for Unix/Linux over SSH, not Windows WMI.
distractor_notes.B: SNMP is for network devices, not full Windows host discovery.
distractor_notes.C: Anonymous/guest access can't read the WMI data discovery needs.

stem: What does an organization gain by converting a legacy business service into an application service?

options.text: A discoverable, maintained dependency map with entry points instead of a static high-level record

rationale: Conversion upgrades a flat business-service record into an application service that Service Mapping can discover and keep current — with entry points and a real dependency topology. That topology is what enables impact analysis and change planning.

distractor_notes.A: Credentials are still needed to discover the now-mapped service.
distractor_notes.B: Conversion adds discovered detail; it doesn't reduce CI counts as a goal.
distractor_notes.C: It doesn't delete incidents.

stem: A team wants role-based access and rollup reporting across a set of related application services. Which construct supports this?
rationale: Service Groups bundle related application services so you can manage access and report on them as a unit. They're the organizational layer that turns many individual maps into a manageable portfolio.

distractor_notes.B: Identifier entries handle CI matching, not service grouping.
distractor_notes.C: Process classifiers route processes to patterns; they don't group services.
distractor_notes.D: Tag categories define tag values for tag-based mapping, not service portfolios.

stem: A connection Service Mapping won't auto-discover should still appear on the map. What lets you add it deliberately?

options.text: Add it as an inclusion (manual connection) on the map

rationale: Inclusions let you manually add a CI or connection the automated discovery can't find — say a dependency reached over an unsupported protocol. It complements automatic discovery so the map reflects reality even where patterns can't reach.

distractor_notes.A: The heartbeat checks availability; it doesn't add connections.
distractor_notes.B: Disabling the schedule stops rediscovery; it doesn't add a connection.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting a CI removes data rather than adding the missing link.

stem: Which capability generates entry point or connection candidates from observed NetFlow and netstat traffic data?
rationale: Traffic-based connection discovery analyzes flow data (NetFlow/netstat) to infer who talks to whom, surfacing candidate connections and entry points that pure pattern discovery might miss. It's how Service Mapping fills gaps from observed network behavior.

distractor_notes.A: Health remediation fixes data quality; it doesn't read traffic flows.
distractor_notes.B: Data certification is a human attestation control, unrelated to flow analysis.
distractor_notes.C: Credential affinity remembers working credentials, not traffic.

stem: To minimize failed logins and account lockouts during a large Service Mapping rollout, what credential practice helps most?

options.text: Store credentials on each target host
Scope credentials to the right CI types/IP ranges and rely on credential affinity
Use one universal admin credential everywhere with no scope
Disable credential affinity to retry every credential each run

rationale: Scoping credentials to where they apply, plus affinity that remembers what worked, means the MID Server tries the right credential first instead of cycling through many. That dramatically cuts failed authentications and the lockouts they can trigger.

distractor_notes.A: Storing secrets on hosts is insecure and unsupported.
distractor_notes.C: An unscoped universal credential maximizes wrong-credential attempts and lockout risk.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling affinity forces retrying every credential — the opposite of what reduces lockouts.

stem: To start mapping a web-based business service, you must tell Service Mapping where users enter it. What do you define?

options.text: An entry point (such as a URL or host:port)

rationale: An entry point defines where a service is accessed (URL, load balancer, host:port) and is the seed Service Mapping uses to begin top-down discovery of the service's tiers.

distractor_notes.B: Reconciliation rules govern attribute authority, not where mapping starts.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: Reports measure data; they don't seed a map.

stem: You need to onboard hundreds of services and don't want to create each entry point by hand. What is the efficient approach?

options.text: Create each entry point manually one at a time

rationale: Service Mapping supports importing entry points in bulk (for example, from a file), which scales onboarding of many services far better than manual creation.

distractor_notes.B: Manual creation doesn't scale to hundreds of services.
distractor_notes.C: Without entry points, top-down mapping has no seed.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists handle notifications.

stem: To map the internals of a database tier, Service Mapping must authenticate to the application itself, not just the OS. Which credential type enables this?
rationale: Applicative credentials let Service Mapping log in at the application level (for example, into a database) to discover internal configuration that OS credentials alone can't reach.

distractor_notes.B: OS credentials get you onto the host but not into the app's internals.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation rules manage attribute authority.

stem: Service maps drift as infrastructure changes. How do you keep them current without manual re-runs?

options.text: Re-map everything by hand each week

rationale: Scheduling automated map maintenance triggers periodic rediscovery so maps stay accurate as the environment changes, avoiding manual upkeep.

distractor_notes.B: Manual weekly re-mapping is unsustainable.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling Service Mapping abandons the maps.
distractor_notes.D: Thresholds don't refresh maps.

stem: A shared monitoring agent appears on many maps and clutters them without adding value. How do you keep it off the maps?

options.text: Exclude the CI from the maps
Delete the CI from the CMDB
Add it to a watch list

rationale: Map exclusions let you keep specific CIs out of service maps (and set boundaries on how far mapping traverses), reducing noise without deleting the CI from the CMDB.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting the CI removes legitimate inventory; exclusion is targeted.
distractor_notes.C: Watch lists handle notifications.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling IRE harms identification.

stem: An older, manually created business service should become a properly mapped Application Service. What action accomplishes this?

options.text: Convert the service to an application service
Delete it and hope Discovery recreates it

rationale: Service Mapping provides a way to convert existing services into application services so they can be mapped and maintained with the modern model, preserving continuity.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting risks losing context and isn't the supported conversion.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: Read-only doesn't change the service type or map it.

stem: In a cloud environment, services are best identified by resource tags rather than fixed entry points. Which Service Mapping approach suits this?
rationale: Tag-based services use cloud resource tags to define and group what belongs to a service, fitting dynamic cloud environments better than static entry points.

distractor_notes.B: Fixed host:port entry points don't fit elastic, tag-driven cloud resources.
distractor_notes.C: Reconciliation rules govern attribute authority.
distractor_notes.D: Coalesce matches import records.

stem: Before declaring maps production-ready, a team wants to review which application services mapped successfully and which need attention. Which tool helps?
rationale: The Application Service Readiness dashboard shows the mapping status/quality of application services, helping teams find and fix problem maps before go-live.

distractor_notes.B: The Service Catalog is for ordering services.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form behavior.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists handle notifications.

stem: You want a set of application services to be grouped automatically based on criteria rather than maintained by hand. Which feature fits?
rationale: Dynamic CI groups define membership by query/criteria, so services are grouped automatically and stay current as CIs change — less manual maintenance than static lists.

distractor_notes.B: Static lists require manual upkeep and go stale.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation rules manage attribute authority.

stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between a business service and an entry point in Service Mapping?

options.text: The entry point is where mapping of the service begins and seeds discovery of its dependencies
The entry point replaces the CMDB
A business service cannot have an entry point

rationale: An entry point is attached to the service as the seed for top-down mapping; from it, Service Mapping discovers the underlying dependencies that make up the service.

distractor_notes.B: They are directly related — the entry point seeds the service's map.
distractor_notes.C: The entry point doesn't replace the CMDB; results populate it.
distractor_notes.D: Business/application services have entry points to be mapped.

stem: Which TWO help keep service maps accurate and useful over time?

options.text: Excluding noisy CIs that add no value
Deleting the application service after mapping

rationale: Periodic rediscovery keeps maps current, and excluding noise keeps them readable and relevant. Removing credentials would break discovery, and deleting the service destroys the map.

distractor_notes.C: Without credentials, Service Mapping can't access targets.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting the application service removes the map you built.

stem: Which TWO are valid ways to create entry points for Service Mapping?

options.text: Define them manually for a service
Import them in bulk from a file
Generate them from a UI policy
Derive them from a watch list

rationale: Entry points can be created manually per service or imported in bulk for scale. UI policies and watch lists have nothing to do with entry-point creation.

distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form behavior, not entry points.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists handle notifications.
